newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Megawati vows to continue legal fight.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Megawati vows to continue legal fight.

text.p: Ousted Indonesian minority party leader Megawati Sukarnoputri said court verdicts this week against her supporters were unfair, but vowed to continue using the law to recover her lost political status.
"I will carry on," Megawati told reporters late on Wednesday night at her home as she waited for the last of 124 supporters to be released from prison.
The daughter of Indonesia's founding president, Sukarno, she was ousted as leader of the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) by a government-backed faction in June.

The Central Jakarta State Court sentenced 115 of her supporters on Wednesday to four months and three days in jail for disobeying police orders to disperse on July 27, the day the worst riots in two decades rocked Jakarta.
The court dismissed prosecution allegations of assault against them, and acquitted nine of both charges.
All those still in custody were released after spending almost all the sentence period in custody after their arrest.

The confrontation started after Megawati was ousted as PDI leader. Her adherents occupied the PDI headquarters in central Jakarta to prevent its takeover by the rival faction headed by Deputy Parliamentary Speaker Surjadi.
Surjadi's supporters, backed by police, stormed the building on July 27, sparking rioting in which five people died and dozens of buildings were burned or damaged.
Defence lawyers protested that none of Surjadi's supporters who attacked the building were detained by the hundreds of police present at the time.

Megawati told reporters she wanted to demonstrate to Indonesians how the legal system in the country worked. She said she and her supporters had filed more than 100 lawsuits around the country challenging her removal as PDI leader.

Referring to Wednesday's court decision, she said: "The verdicts handed down today were not fair. It was very clear from our defence and witnesses that it was not balanced and the facts were turned upside down."
But she has vowed to continue using the courts, saying she wanted to show Indonesia should be based on the rule of law rather than political power.
Political analysts have said the government moved to sideline Megawati and her supporters because they feared she could draw votes away from the ruling Golkar party in general elections next May.
Only three parties -- Golkar, the Christian-nationalist PDI and the Moslem-oriented United Development Party -- are legally permitted to contest the elections.
